source_refs.note: Book p. 79-80: 5.1.2 Improper Rational Fraction (definition, four examples, long division box, identity remark) and the theorem on equal polynomials with its example (PDF 85). Tables, Teaching notes, Key points, Common mistakes are ours.

blocks.text: A rational fraction \(\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}\) is called an Improper Rational Fraction if the degree of the polynomial \(P(x)\) in the numerator is equal to or greater than the degree of the polynomial \(Q(x)\) in the denominator.
For example, \(\frac{x}{2x-3}\), \(\frac{(x-2)(x+1)}{(x-1)(x+4)}\), \(\frac{x^{2}-3}{3x+1}\) and \(\frac{x^{3}-x^{2}+x+1}{x^{2}+5}\) are improper rational fractions or improper fractions.

blocks.caption: Checking the book's four improper fractions

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Improper means "top degree \(\ge\) bottom degree". Equal degrees already make a fraction improper, just as \(\frac{4}{4}\) and \(\frac{7}{4}\) are improper fractions in arithmetic.
Any improper rational fraction can be reduced by division to a mixed form, consisting of the sum of a polynomial and a proper rational fraction.

For example, \(\frac{3x^{2}+1}{x-2}\) is an improper rational fraction. By long division we obtain
\[\dfrac{3x^{2}+1}{x-2} = 3x + 6 + \dfrac{13}{x-2}\]

blocks.text_alt: Long division: x minus 2 into 3 x squared plus 1. Quotient 3 x plus 6. First subtract plus or minus 3 x squared, minus or plus 6 x, leaving 6 x plus 1. Then subtract plus or minus 6 x and 12, leaving the remainder 13.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In the book's division box the second subtraction row is printed as \(\pm 6x \;\; 12\): the sign of 12 is lost. Since \(6(x-2) = 6x - 12\), the row is \(\pm 6x \mp 12\), and \((6x + 1) - (6x - 12) = 13\). The quotient \(3x + 6\) and the remainder 13 are correct.

blocks.text_alt: Long division: x minus 2 into 3 x squared plus 1. Quotient 3 x plus 6. First subtract plus or minus 3 x squared, minus or plus 6 x, leaving 6 x plus 1. Then subtract plus or minus 6 x, minus or plus 12, leaving the remainder 13.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
How the long division works, row by row:
1. Divide the first term \(3x^{2}\) by the first term \(x\) of the divisor: \(3x\). Write it on top.
2. Multiply: \(3x(x - 2) = 3x^{2} - 6x\). Subtract it (change both signs and add): \((3x^{2} + 1) - (3x^{2} - 6x) = 6x + 1\).
3. Divide again: \(6x \div x = 6\). Write \(+6\) on top.
4. Multiply: \(6(x - 2) = 6x - 12\). Subtract: \((6x + 1) - (6x - 12) = 13\).
5. The remainder 13 has degree 0, less than the degree 1 of \(x - 2\), so we stop.
The upper signs (\(\pm\), \(\mp\)) show the row being subtracted; the lower signs show it after changing signs. Leaving a gap for the missing \(x\) term in \(3x^{2} + 1\) keeps like terms in the same column.
Result: dividend = divisor × quotient + remainder, so \(\frac{3x^{2}+1}{x-2} = 3x + 6 + \frac{13}{x-2}\).
i.e., an improper rational fraction has \(\frac{3x^{2} - 1}{x - 2}\) been reduced to the sum of a polynomial \(3x + 6\) and a proper rational fraction \(\frac{13}{x - 2}\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints \(\frac{3x^{2} - 1}{x - 2}\) here. The fraction that was divided is \(\frac{3x^{2} + 1}{x - 2}\) (with \(3x^{2} - 1\) the remainder would be 11, not 13). The sentence should read: the improper rational fraction \(\frac{3x^{2} + 1}{x - 2}\) has been reduced to the sum of the polynomial \(3x + 6\) and the proper rational fraction \(\frac{13}{x - 2}\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Check: put \(x = 3\). Left side: \(\frac{3(9) + 1}{3 - 2} = 28\). Right side: \(3(3) + 6 + \frac{13}{1} = 9 + 6 + 13 = 28\). Equal.
Why divide at all? The method of 5.1.3 works only on proper fractions. So for an improper fraction we first divide, keep the polynomial part as it is, and resolve only the proper part into partial fractions.
When a rational fraction is separated into partial fractions, the result is an identity; i.e., it is true for all values of the variable in the domain of identity.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: The "domain of identity" means all values of \(x\) for which both sides are defined. For \(\frac{3x^{2}+1}{x-2} = 3x + 6 + \frac{13}{x-2}\) that is every \(x \ne 2\), because at \(x = 2\) the denominator is zero.
The evaluation of the coefficients of the partial fractions is based on the following theorem:
"If two polynomials are equal for all values of the variable, then the polynomials have same degree and the coefficients of like powers of the variable in both the polynomials must be equal".

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
How the example is read: the two sides are equal for all \(x\) (\(\forall\, x\) means "for all \(x\)"), so we match the coefficients of each power of \(x\):
\[x^{3}:\ p = 2\]
\[x^{2}:\ q = -3\]
\[x:\ -a = -4 \Rightarrow a = 4\]
\[\text{constant}:\ b = 5\]
Notice \(a = 4\), not \(-4\): the left side carries \(-ax\), so we compare \(-a\) with \(-4\).
Why the theorem is true: subtracting, \((p-2)x^{3} + (q+3)x^{2} + (4-a)x + (b-5) = 0\) for every \(x\). A non-zero polynomial of degree 3 can be zero for at most 3 values of \(x\), so all its coefficients must be 0.
This is the tool of 5.1.3: after clearing denominators we get two equal polynomials and compare coefficients to find the unknown numerators.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}\) is improper when degree of \(P(x)\) \(\ge\) degree of \(Q(x)\); equal degrees count as improper.
2. Long division turns an improper fraction into polynomial + proper fraction: \(\frac{3x^{2}+1}{x-2} = 3x + 6 + \frac{13}{x-2}\).
3. Only the proper part is resolved into partial fractions.
4. A partial fraction result is an identity, true for every \(x\) where both sides are defined.
5. Equal polynomials have the same degree and equal coefficients of like powers.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.text:
1. Treating equal degrees as proper: \(\frac{x}{2x-3}\) must be divided first.
2. Forgetting the gap for a missing power in long division (\(3x^{2} + 1\) has no \(x\) term), so unlike terms are subtracted from each other.
3. Subtracting only the first term of a row: \((6x + 1) - (6x - 12) = 13\), not \(-11\).
4. In \(-ax = -4x\), writing \(a = -4\): compare the whole coefficient, \(-a = -4\), so \(a = 4\).
